The paint laboratory

Explore, connect and evaluate

Suggested teaching time
5–6 weeks

Timing, task steps and quantities are classroom suggestions, not NZQA grade requirements.

Read the standard (PDF)

The brief

How might changing the way I paint change the feeling of my subject?

Investigate your own subject through a practical painting inquiry. Try different processes, connect the discoveries and refine your intentions through further trials. Your evidence should show thinking in progress: the decisions and experiments that inform future artwork.

Materials & preparation

A3 paper or workbook, your own observed objects or photographs, drawing media, water-based paints, brushes, masking materials and a camera for recording larger trials.

Use your own drawings and photographs as starting points. Record sources and seek permission for people, places and culturally significant material. Discuss tikanga and context with your teacher where relevant.

This is an external standard. Use the activities as teaching suggestions; make your own decisions during assessed work. Your teacher must keep support within NZQA’s annual conditions.

Suggested size & quantity

Use these ranges to plan your studio time and materials with your teacher. They are classroom suggestions, not NZQA minimums, maximums or grade requirements. Adapt them to your idea, working pace and access needs.

Practical experiments

Aim for about 10–14 related trials: 6–8 initial process or convention experiments, followed by 4–6 further trials that connect and refine useful discoveries. A6–A5 tests keep experimentation manageable; use an A4 study when a process needs more space.

Workbook

Organise the selected trials across about 6–8 A3 pages. Place related tests together with short notes about what changed, what you discovered and what you will try next. Photograph larger or textured trials clearly.

Selecting evidence

Keep the focus on developmental work rather than adding a finished painting. The suggested number of trials is flexible; check Presentation & submission below for the separate annual limits on submitted pages and formats.

One workbook page means one side of a sheet; a two-page spread counts as two pages. A3 is 297 × 420 mm, A4 is 210 × 297 mm, A5 is 148 × 210 mm and A6 is 105 × 148 mm. Two A4 pages offer about the same area as one A3 page for planning; this does not change any external submission format. Mount small studies or use clear photographs of separate works rather than making everything twice.

Artist connections

Choose the connections that serve your intention. The contemporary models offer different approaches; select a relevant comparison rather than studying every artist. These works are references, not assessment exemplars.

Try a contrast between flat colour, gestural paint and layered marks. Evaluate the results against your own intention rather than aiming to reproduce an artist’s finished image.

  • Ayesha Green

    Contemporary Māori · Aotearoa New Zealand

    Green’s flattened colour and still-life subjects open questions about representation, whenua and national identity. Read the context before comparing how an object can carry a public story and a personal association.

    McCahon House · Still Life education resource (PDF) · Painting investigation

  • Emily Karaka

    Contemporary Māori · Aotearoa New Zealand

    Karaka’s energetic colour, gesture and text connect painting with whenua, whānau and Māori sovereignty. Investigate how the marks carry a political and personal position; read that position alongside the painted surface.

    Sharjah Art Foundation · Ka Awatea, A New Dawn · Painting investigation

  • Jadé Fadojutimi

    Contemporary · United Kingdom

    Look closely at the colour relationships, layered marks and shifting forms in Fadojutimi’s paintings, then watch Tate’s studio film. Consider how everyday experiences and personal interests can become starting points for abstract painting.

    Artist’s official website · paintings · Painting investigation

  • Frances Hodgkins

    Aotearoa New Zealand / Britain

    Look at how still-life objects and landscape can share a painted space. Try shifting the relationship between an object, its surroundings and its colour.

    Christchurch Art Gallery · Still Life

Studio sequence

Use this as a flexible route through the learning. Let the work suggest the next move.

  1. Set an intention

    Choose a subject you can observe and an idea, mood or narrative to investigate. Record your own imagery. Look at the artist resources to identify processes worth testing; the intention remains yours.

  2. Experiment with a question

    Try a manageable set of related experiments: for example, change paint opacity, edge handling or colour temperature while keeping your subject recognisable. Record the material and process beside each test.

  3. Connect the discoveries

    Compare the results. Select a useful relationship between two trials, such as a transparent ground and an opaque silhouette, and test it in a new study. Explain how the connection supports or changes your intention.

  4. Evaluate through making

    Identify a limitation in a promising study. Make a further version that addresses it, then compare the versions. Repeat where useful. Show your reasoning through visual changes and concise, independently written reflections.

  5. Select the development evidence

    Choose the experiments that make your inquiry legible. Order them so someone can see your intention, connections, revisions and changed thinking. Keep the evidence developmental; a collection of finished paintings alone will conceal the inquiry.

A useful studio conversation

Put two related works side by side. Describe what changed, show the evidence and explain what you will investigate next. Invite feedback, then make your own decision.

Presentation & submission

The 2026 workbook route uses eight single-sided A3 pages, digitised into one PDF. A slideshow alternative is limited to eight slides and 120 seconds. Include developmental evidence rather than resolved works. Your teacher manages verification submission; the submitted evidence must be self-contained.

Read the full 2026 NZQA specifications (PDF) and external assessment conditions. These are year-specific requirements; confirm any updates for your assessment year.

What changes between grades?

Student-friendly guidance adapted from the standard. The whole body of relevant evidence determines the grade; the examples below illustrate possibilities.

Grade distinctions for AS91914
GradeWhat the evidence needs to show
AchievementExperiment with materials, techniques and processes in relation to your intention.In this task: Tests investigate how paint choices might communicate the intended mood or idea.
MeritDevelop several approaches and connect experiments to generate possibilities.In this task: A later trial combines discoveries from earlier tests for a clear reason.
ExcellenceEvaluate and refine processes through repeated making and thoughtful selection.In this task: A comparison identifies a limitation; a changed trial addresses it and helps sharpen the intention.

Authority: NZQA AS91914 achievement criteria and explanatory notes (PDF).

Watch for

A list of techniques is not evaluation. Show what changed because of the experiments.

Pause & reflect

Which experiment changed your intention most? Explain what you retained, what you rejected and which visual evidence led to that decision.

Planning, assessment & differentiation

Use process demonstrations and generic practice before assessment. During assessed production, keep assistance within NZQA’s permitted conferencing and authenticity conditions. Students must select and reflect independently; do not prescribe a page-by-page response or supply wording for annotations. The activities here are teaching invitations, not a mandated submission template.

Support and stretch

For teaching practice, reduce the number of simultaneous choices, model one material process and invite oral discussion alongside drawing. Offer vocabulary prompts and accessible media. To extend the learning, ask students to compare alternatives, justify a rejection or investigate a consequence of their own decision. Adapt assessed support to the standard’s conditions and any approved arrangements.

Before issuing the task

Set local start and finish dates, agree available materials and check the current standard, conditions and exemplars. Use school authenticity processes and your normal moderation procedures. Adjust this brief to the class and context; it has not been quality assured by NZQA.
